title: Brick stitch
subtitle: Rows of straight stitches offset like brickwork to cover large areas evenly
excerpt: Brick stitch fills a shape with rows of straight stitches where each row offsets by half a stitch length, like bricks in a wall. The result is a flat, even fill that covers the fabric without the lustrous sheen of satin stitch. It is efficient for large backgrounds.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), flat filling stitches chapter (Project Gutenberg #20776). Weldon's Practical Needlework, Vol. 2 (1886), brick filling entry.

glossaryTerms.definition: The alternating alignment of each row of stitches, where the start of each row is set half a stitch length back from the one above. This creates the brick-like interlocking pattern.

heroPrompt: Brick stitch in two tones of rust and terracotta stranded cotton filling a square ground area, showing the offset brick pattern and even coverage, natural light.

content.text: Brick stitch achieves its even coverage through a
between rows. The first row sets the stitch length. Every subsequent row begins half a stitch length in from the row above, staggering the joins so they look like laid brickwork.
Work the first row of straight stitches across the top of the shape, spacing them evenly at the chosen stitch length.
Begin the second row half a stitch length in from the first stitch of row one. Work stitches of the same length.
Begin the third row aligned with the first row. Continue alternating the offset each row.
Bring each stitch up between the bases of the row above to keep the coverage solid.

items.cause: The second row is starting at the wrong position.
items.fix: The needle for each row must emerge between the bases of the stitches above. If the row below has gaps at its base, the coverage will fail.

items.cause: The half-drop offset is not being maintained consistently.
items.fix: Mark the start points of each row on the fabric before stitching. A ruler and water-soluble pen make this fast.

content.text: Brick stitch is widely used as a background fill in crewelwork and canvas work. When worked in graduated colours from one row to the next, it gives a striped shaded effect similar to long and short stitch but with harder colour breaks.
